examples.title: See The Difference
examples.subtitle: Transform vague requests into precise, results-driven prompts

example1.before: Write a blog post about productivity
example1.after: As an experienced content strategist, write a 1,200-word blog post about productivity hacks for remote workers. Target audience: tech professionals aged 25-40. Tone: Professional yet approachable. Include 5 actionable tips with real examples.

example2.after: As a senior marketing consultant, create a 3-email welcome sequence for new subscribers to a meditation app. Audience: stressed professionals seeking work-life balance. Tone: Calm and empathetic. Each email should be 150-200 words with a clear CTA.

example3.after: As a social media expert, create 5 Instagram captions for a sustainable fashion brand launching eco-friendly sneakers. Target: environmentally conscious millennials. Tone: Inspiring and authentic. Include relevant hashtags and emojis.

example4.after: As a patient educator, explain quantum computing to a 12-year-old with no technical background. Use simple analogies from everyday life. Keep it under 300 words. Make it engaging and avoid jargon completely.

example5.after: As a B2B sales expert, write a cold outreach email to CTOs of mid-sized tech companies introducing our cybersecurity solution. Tone: Professional and value-focused. Length: 150 words max. Include a clear meeting request CTA.

step1.title: What are you trying to achieve?
step1.subtitle: Be specific about your goal. The clearer you are, the better the result.
step1.placeholder: e.g., Write a blog post about sustainable living
step1.learnMoreDesc: This is your main goal or objective. Think of it as the 'what' you want the AI to create or help you with. Be clear and specific — vague requests lead to vague results.
examples: Write a product description for eco-friendly water bottles
Create a marketing email for a new app launch
Generate ideas for social media posts about productivity

step2.title: Who's your audience?
step2.subtitle: This helps the AI understand who you're writing for and tailor the response.
step2.placeholder: e.g., Tech-savvy millennials interested in sustainability
step2.learnMoreDesc: Context provides background information that shapes the AI's understanding. This includes your audience, situation, constraints, or any relevant details. The more context you provide, the more tailored and useful the response will be.
examples: Small business owners looking to grow their online presence
Students learning programming for the first time
Busy parents seeking meal planning tips

step3.title: Which AI are you using?
step3.subtitle: Different AIs have different strengths. This helps tailor your prompt.
step3.learnMoreDesc: Different AI models have unique strengths and formatting preferences. ChatGPT excels at creative and conversational tasks. Claude is great for detailed analysis. Gemini handles multimodal tasks well.

step4.title: What tone should the output have?
step4.subtitle: Tone shapes how your AI responds. Choose what fits your audience. (Optional - you can skip this)
step4.learnMoreDesc: Tone determines the personality and style of the AI's response. It affects word choice, sentence structure, and overall feel. Match the tone to your audience and purpose for maximum impact.

step5.title: Any special rules or requirements?
step5.subtitle: Special instructions help shape precision. Add formatting needs or content limits.
step5.placeholder: e.g., Keep it under 500 words, use bullet points, include 3 examples
step5.learnMoreTitle: When do I need special rules?
step5.learnMoreDesc: Requirements and constraints define the boundaries and format of the output. This includes word limits, structural preferences (bullet points, headings), must-have elements, or things to avoid.
examples: Keep under 500 words, use bullet points

step6.title: What role should the AI play?
step6.subtitle: This tells the AI how to act and what perspective to use.
step6.placeholder: e.g., Expert marketer, helpful teacher, creative writer
step6.learnMoreDesc: Assigning a role gives the AI a persona and expertise level to embody. This shapes its perspective, knowledge base, and approach.
examples: Senior marketing consultant with 10 years experience
Patient educator who explains complex topics simply
Creative copywriter specializing in emotional storytelling

step7.title: How should the output be formatted?
step7.subtitle: Choosing a format shapes how the AI structures its response.
step7.learnMoreDesc: Output format tells the AI how to structure its response. Bullet lists are great for quick scanning, numbered steps for processes, narrative for storytelling, and tables for comparisons. When in doubt, let the AI decide.

step8.title: What's failed before? (Optional)
step8.subtitle: If you've tried AI for this and got bad results, tell us what went wrong. We'll turn it into hard prohibitions.
step8.placeholder: e.g., It used too much corporate jargon. The output was too generic. It listed features instead of benefits.
step8.learnMoreDesc: Telling the AI what NOT to do is often more powerful than describing what you want. Your failed attempts become explicit prohibitions in the generated prompt, directly preventing those mistakes from happening again.

result.title: Your Expert Prompt is Ready!

result.pasteTip: 💡 This prompt instructs {{aiModel}} on exactly what to write. Paste it in and the AI will produce your final content.

IDENTITY.label: Identity
IDENTITY.techniqueDesc: We specified a precise expert role ({{role}}) with expertise markers and communication style. This activates the model's training data associated with expert-level outputs in this specific domain.
IDENTITY.why: LLMs are trained on vast amounts of text. A generic role triggers a broad, average distribution. Specifying an expert role (like the one we built for your task: '{{role}}') signals a very specific corpus — high-stakes professional writing. The model literally draws from different patterns than it would for a general query.
IDENTITY.after:
### [IDENTITY]
You are {{role}}.
Your communication style is {{tone}}.
You have direct experience with {{task}}.
IDENTITY.without: Without role priming, the model defaults to its 'helpful assistant' persona — generically competent, deliberately cautious, and optimized for the statistically average user. You'll get polished mediocrity: correct sentences but weak, average decisions.
IDENTITY.modify: Try changing the operational context clause. Swap 'professional' for 'provocative' or 'academic' and see how the entire tone shifts while the task stays identical. That's role priming in action.

CONTEXT.label: Context
CONTEXT.techniqueDesc: This block gives the model the complete situational triangle: what's happening, who reads the output, and what they do with it. This prevents the model from filling context gaps with its own assumptions.
CONTEXT.why: Without explicit context, the model writes for its internal 'most likely user' — a statistical average. Specifying audience and downstream use triangulates the target. The 'This output will be used for' line is particularly powerful: it changes expected length, formality level, and whether the model uses placeholders.
CONTEXT.without: The model makes confident but generic assumptions about your audience. For a product description, it assumes a general consumer. For an email, it assumes a corporate context. These defaults are specifically wrong for most actual situations.
CONTEXT.modify: The highest-leverage modification is 'The audience for your output.' Change it from 'general public' to 'technical experts' and the vocabulary, depth, and framing shift completely — same task, different output.

TASK.label: Task
TASK.techniqueDesc: Instead of a single instruction, the task is broken into sequential reasoning steps. Each step builds on the previous one, forcing the model to approach the problem in a structured way.
TASK.why: LLMs generate text token by token. When Step 1 instructs the model to analyze before writing, the output of that analysis influences the token probabilities for everything that follows. It mimics how a human expert works: analyze first, structure second, write third.
TASK.after:
### [TASK]
Step 1: Analyze {{task}} for key triggers.
Step 2: Draft the response based on Step 1.
Step 3: Refine and finalize.
TASK.without: The model produces output in a single pass — which means it's simultaneously deciding what to say, how to structure it, and what words to use. The result is output that sounds fluent but lacks strategic structure or depth.
TASK.modify: Change what Step 1 asks the model to identify before writing. 'Identify emotional triggers' vs 'Identify technical constraints' produce structurally different outputs even with identical writing instructions.

OUTPUT_STRUCTURE.label: Output Structure
OUTPUT_STRUCTURE.techniqueDesc: Exact section names, lengths, and exclusions eliminate all format interpretation. 'Structure your response exactly as follows' is a hard constraint that tells the model this is a rule, not a suggestion.
OUTPUT_STRUCTURE.why: Without explicit structure specification, the model generates whatever layout it considers most 'typical' for the task. Named sections with maximum lengths give the model hard boundaries it respects. It also understands that a section named 'Executive Summary' needs to perform a specific rhetorical function different from 'Technical Appendix'.
OUTPUT_STRUCTURE.after:
### [OUTPUT STRUCTURE]
Structure your response exactly as follows:
[Intro]: max 100 words
[Body]: 3 bullet points
Do not include: meta-commentary.
OUTPUT_STRUCTURE.without: You get 2-3 paragraphs of flowing text with no structure. Even when the content is excellent, you can't control whether you get bullets, headers, or whether the model adds an unsolicited 'In conclusion' paragraph.
OUTPUT_STRUCTURE.modify: 'Do not include' is the most underused lever. Exclude pricing disclaimers, meta-commentary, or call-to-action boilerplate to force the model to focus only on the high-value content you actually need.

EXEMPLAR.label: Exemplar
EXEMPLAR.techniqueDesc: Showing the model an example of target output quality. The model reverse-engineers the style, register, and implicit quality standards from the example and applies them — learning by demonstration.
EXEMPLAR.why: LLMs learn by pattern matching. An example anchors ambiguities like 'professional tone' or 'engaging opening' to concrete text. The model identifies stylistic patterns and sentence length norms that are impossible to describe perfectly in words.
EXEMPLAR.after:
### [EXEMPLAR]
Here is an example of the quality I want:
"Build your network before you need it. High-value connections take time..."
EXEMPLAR.without: The model interprets your instructions at the level of their literal meaning. 'Professional tone' means something different to the model than to you. An example anchors all of these ambiguities simultaneously to your specific standard.
EXEMPLAR.modify: Swap the exemplar style while keeping the task constant. Replace a formal example with an informal/punchy one. The entire output character shifts while following the same task instructions.

CONSTRAINT.label: Constraint
CONSTRAINT.techniqueDesc: Constraints are split into non-negotiable rules (Hard) and strong preferences (Soft). This tells the model exactly where it has flexibility and where it doesn't, preventing it from trading off the wrong things.
CONSTRAINT.why: Hard constraints signal inviolability. Soft constraints give the model permission to be contextually flexible. In long prompts with many requirements, this split is what prevents the model from compromising on a critical requirement to satisfy a style preference.
CONSTRAINT.after:
### [CONSTRAINT]
Hard constraints:
- Under 200 words
Soft constraints:
- Use a friendly, approachable tone
CONSTRAINT.without: The model treats all instructions as equally weighted preferences. In a complex prompt, it may prioritize sounding 'friendly' over staying under the word count limit. You lose control over which rules are truly inviolable.
CONSTRAINT.modify: Move constraints between Hard and Soft to change the model's priority. If output runs too long, move 'word count' to Hard — the model will sacrifice style to ensure it stays within the length requirement.
